message.content:
I don’t have real‑time data, but you can quickly check the current air quality in Los Angeles using a few reliable resources:

| Source | How to use it | What you’ll see |
|--------|---------------|-----------------|
| **AirNow** (U.S. EPA) | Go to [airnow.gov](https://www.airnow.gov/), enter “Los Angeles” or your ZIP code. | Current AQI value, pollutant breakdown (PM₂.₅, PM₁₀, O₃, NO₂, CO), and health advisories. |
| **AQICN** (World Air Quality Index) | Visit [aqicn.org](https://aqicn.org/city/los-angeles/). | Live AQI, trend graphs, and forecast for the next 24 h. |
| **Local news sites** (e.g., LA Times, KABC) | Search “LA air quality” on their websites. | Often include a quick snapshot and links to official data. |
| **Mobile apps** (AirVisual, Plume Labs) | Download from App Store/Google Play and set your location. | Real‑time AQI, alerts, and historical trends. |

**Typical LA air quality:**  
- **Spring & early summer**: Often moderate to unhealthy‑for‑sensitive‑groups due to wildfire smoke and ozone.  
- **Fall & winter**: Usually better, but can still be affected by wildfires in the region.  

If you’re planning outdoor activities, it’s a good idea to check the AQI at least a few hours before you head out. If the AQI is 101–150 (“Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups”), consider limiting strenuous exercise. If it’s 151–200 (“Unhealthy”), stay indoors if possible. For anything above 201 (“Very Unhealthy”) or 301+ (“Hazardous”), it’s best to avoid outdoor exposure entirely.
